texts: good. the question asks what kind of thing mire-essence is, and the query leaves exactly that slot open on the kind itself, so any statement saying what mire-essence is a kind of will answer it; nothing is added to the knowledge base.

good. the query puts the unknown in the individual slot of the fused role-title kind chief_keeper — exactly the atom a matching statement ("X is the chief Keeper") stores — and the answer comes back bare, unbound by any name.
How many lanterns are there in Aelmere?

good. the query builds the group of lanterns, leaves its count open where "how many" asks, and ties that group to Aelmere by the static containment relation your "in" states rather than by an event location.
Where does the Stilllight Lantern stand?

mixed: the query is faithful - "stand" is correctly treated as a position, not a happening, and the lantern is bound by its name - but "where ... stand" can only find a position recorded as containment ("in / at / inside / within"). A position written with any other preposition ("on the quay", "beside the mere") has no form this question can reach, so it would come back empty rather than wrong. If the lantern's position is stated with a non-containment preposition, ask with that same preposition - "What does the Stilllight Lantern stand on?" - and if it is stated as being in a place, leave the question exactly as it is.
What hunts nightmoths at a lantern-row?

good. the hunter is the bare wh-answer in the hunting event's agent slot, the prey stays a kind-level object the hunting does not change, and the lantern-row binds by its kind in the location slot with no tense atom, which is right for the generic present.

bad: the query hangs the unknown on a literal "for"-phrase attached to the using event instead of asking for that event's purpose, so it answers only if the stored fact happens to be worded with "for" and misses a purpose stated as "salt-bloom is used to cure hides" — the wording the reasoner actually recognizes as a purpose. Ask the reason of a plainly named focus event instead: "Why is salt-bloom used?" — that routes through the canonical reason link, which stated purposes feed into, so it reaches both a purpose and a cause. Word the answering fact with a purpose infinitive ("Salt-bloom is used to preserve fish") rather than "used for preserving fish", since a "for"-phrase purpose is not reachable as a purpose.

good. the query leaves the harvesting event's time slot open and binds salt-bloom as the thing harvested, with no doer invented for the agentless passive and no tense forced onto the habitual present.

good. the query mirrors the way a bare-plural generic is stored — a rule giving each sky-cat its own roosting — and puts the unknown in that roosting's place slot, which is exactly what the question asks.
When do sky-cats descend from the cliff-spires?
good. the query asks for the time of a descending whose doer is a sky-cat and whose starting point is the cliff-spires, with the unknown in the time slot and nothing added beyond the question.
How many solo nights does an apprentice complete before the Council assigns that apprentice to a station?

(: $prf (And (Member $a apprentice) (Member $e1 complete) (Agent $e1 $a) (Theme $e1 $g) (GroupOf $g solo_night) (Cardinality $g $n) (Member $e2 assign) (Agent $e2 $c) (Member $c council) (Theme $e2 $a) (Goal $e2 $s) (Member $s station) (Before $e1 $e2)) $tv)

good. the query counts the group of solo nights the apprentice completes, keeps the same apprentice in the Council's assigning event for "that apprentice", and orders the completing before the assigning as the sentence does.

good. the query asks who does the tending and pins the tended thing to the name "Stilllight Lantern", leaving the answer slot open and adding no tense to the present habitual, so nothing of the question is lost or added. One thing to know: the lantern lands in the "object changed by the action" slot for "tend", so a stored fact that words the same care with a pure maintenance verb ("keeps the Stilllight Lantern") may be filed in the neighbouring slot and not line up.

good. the query binds "the Council" as an ordinary council (capitalized, but the sentence never states a proper name) as the party doing the meeting and leaves the time of the meeting open, with no tense invented for the present habitual. One thing to know: this asks for the meeting's time slot (which day, which hour), not its rate — a fact recorded only as a frequency like "every two weeks" would not come back, so ask "How often does the Council meet?" when the rate is what you want.
What shields the Northcove against the north wind?

good. the shielder is left open as the answer, the Northcove is bound by its name and sits in the "unchanged thing being protected" slot, and "against the north wind" is kept with the preposition the sentence actually uses rather than being folded into some other relation. Nothing is added: the north wind is carried as the one kind "north wind" with no extra claims about it.
When did four wraiths emerge from the Sunken Cove?
good. every part of the question is carried: a group of wraiths of size exactly four, doing the emerging, out of the named Sunken Cove, in the past, with the time left open as the asked-for answer.
How many copper cauldrons are in Cauldron Hall?

good. the query picks out one group of copper cauldrons sitting in the named Cauldron Hall and returns the size of that group, which is exactly what "how many" asks; "are in" is correctly recorded as a standing position rather than as something happening.
Who is the warden of Cauldron Hall?

good. the query asks exactly who the warden is — Cauldron Hall bound by its name and typed as a hall, the unknown left in the warden slot, and the two joined by the ordinary "role-of" link a statement of the same fact would use.
What repels nightmoths from a lantern?

good. the question is asked as a standing habit with the unknown in the doer slot, nightmoths as the kind repelled and the lantern in the whence (from) slot, and nothing added beyond what you asked. One thing to keep steady on your side: a bare answering statement like "smokeleaf repels nightmoths" is filed as a kind-to-kind relation that this question's event shape cannot reach, so keep the lantern in the sentence that answers it.
What is the brass snuffer used for?

good. the passive "is used" is rebuilt with the brass snuffer as the thing used and no doer named, and the ask is for the purpose of that using. Worth knowing on your side: the purpose only binds when the answering statement states it as a clause ("the brass snuffer is used to douse the wick"), not as a noun phrase ("a tool for wick-dousing"), and the snuffer should be named the same way there.
Where does the village cremate the dead?

mixed: the shape is right — the village as the doer, the unknown in the place slot, no tense on a standing practice — but "the dead" has no noun head, and the translator has no rule for an adjective standing in for a noun, so it lands as the bare property symbol `dead`. A statement that wrote the same people as bodies, as corpses, or as a group would then not be reached by this question. Give the phrase a plain one-word noun head and use that same noun in the answering statement: "Where does the village cremate corpses?"

mixed: the count line is the most the instruction set licenses and it does bind a stated count ("three Keepers are active"), but a plural's copular property is normally stored per member ("the Keepers are active") or as a vague count phrase ("several Keepers are active"), and neither leaves a number sitting on the group for this query to read — so the how-many form will usually come back empty. Ask for the Keepers themselves and read the count off the answers: "Which Keepers are active?"
When does a Keeper repeat the phrase?

good. the query leaves the time slot open on the repeating event and binds the Keeper by kind and the phrase by kind, so it asks exactly when a keeper's repeating of the phrase happens, and the unmarked habitual present is carried with no tense atom, as the instruction set prescribes.
What lies under the water in the Sunken Cove?

good. "lies" states a position rather than an event, so the thing asked for sits in the unknown slot of an entity-attached "under" atom over the water, and the Sunken Cove binds by its name as what contains that water — the same attachment a statement worded this way would take.
Who arrived in Aelmere in the late summer of Year 1?

mixed: the arriver is correctly the unknown and the place and year bind, but "the late summer of Year 1" has no licensed time term - the translator had to coin a bare late_summer symbol and lift the year out of the genitive by hand, so the question only matches a statement that happened to be worded the same way ("in the summer of Year 1" or "late in summer" would store something else and the question would miss). Split the two time adjuncts and keep one fixed wording for the season everywhere in the stream: "Who arrived in Aelmere in late summer, in Year 1?" If your world names months, naming the month instead of the season removes the guess entirely, since months are a time term the translator has.

good. the query puts the unknown in the verb slot of an event Tessa Brae is the agent of, binds her by her verbatim name string rather than a guessed symbol, and asserts nothing - the instruction set's prescribed "what does X do?" shape exactly.

good. "Cove Stair" is read as a name (the capitalized run says more than the bare kind word), so the query binds it by its name string and leaves the kind slot open - which is exactly what "what is it?" asks - and nothing is asserted.

good. the query picks out the thing that is an ebb and is deep and leaves the answer slot open, which is the licensed shape for an open "what" ask (the same shape as "what does Bob do?"), so any identifying class stored for it binds. Two limits are ours, not your sentence's, and no rewording would remove them: an open answer slot also re-binds the words you supplied, so "ebb" and "deep" come back alongside a real answer, and we have to guess whether "deep ebb" was recorded split (an ebb that is deep) or fused as a single term of art.

good. the query binds the feather store by its kind and asks what contains it, which is exactly what "where is X?" asks. One caveat on our side: we can only reach a position recorded as containment ("in / at / inside / within"), so if the store's position was stated with "next to", "on" or "atop", this question finds nothing rather than the wrong thing.
Which ground feathers do not ward lanterns?

good. the unknown sits in the warder slot, the warding event and the lanterns are pinned as stated, and the whole pattern is asked at falsity, which is what the negative "which N do not V?" asks. Note only that a fact stated about the kinds at large ("ground feathers ward lanterns") does not distribute to individual feathers, so this instance-level question will stay silent on it rather than guess.
Where does the cold-threshold wind come from?

good. the wind binds by its compound kind, the asked-for origin is the bare unknown in the coming event's source slot, and the wind is the undergoer of the motion rather than a volitional doer, which is the reading a natural force takes.
Whom did the Council invest as a Keeper on day 260 of Year 1?

good. the unknown sits in the object slot of the investing event, the Council stays the investing party, both date terms ride the event, and the conferred Keeper role is rebuilt as the state the investing brought about — the same shape an "invested X as a Keeper" statement is stored in, so the answer binds. It does ask for that full conferred-role bundle, so an appointment recorded some other way (a plain "X was a Keeper from day 260") would not be reached by this question.
Why do the lanterns of Aelmere burn every night?

good. the query asks for the reason of the burning itself, keeps the habitual reading of "every night" (a night slot plus its daily cycle, no tense), and binds both the lantern group and its Aelmere link.
Why does a Keeper light a lantern with mire-essence?

good. the query rebuilds the lighting event exactly as a statement of it would — a keeper as the doer, the lantern as the thing changed, mire-essence as the means — and hangs the reason-ask on that event, asserting nothing.
Why does a Keeper store the mire-essence that forms in the cauldron?
good. the storing is the focus event the reason is asked of, and "that forms in the cauldron" comes through as its own forming event with the mire-essence and the cauldron both in place.
Why do sky-cats descend from the cliff-spires?
good. the query asks the reason for the descending itself, with sky-cats bound generically by kind, the cliff-spires in the whence (from) slot, and no tense on what is a standing habit.
Why does every Keeper consider that sky-cats are sacred?

good. the query rebuilds the attitude as a considering held by a keeper, with "sky-cats are sacred" kept inside it as the held belief rather than asserted, and asks the reason for that considering; the universal "every Keeper" rightly becomes a per-keeper pattern, which is how a distributed member is queried.
Why did the Council create the modern feather-ration system?

good. the query rebuilds the create event with the Council as the doer and the modern feather-ration system as the thing created, and asks only for its reason — nothing is asserted and nothing in the question is dropped.
Why do the Northcove lanterns burn through winter?

mixed: the Northcove lanterns, the burning and the reason-ask all come through, but "through winter" flattens to a bare winter time-stamp, so the question ends up asking why the lanterns burn at some point in winter rather than why they burn the whole season — and it will miss a stored fact that records the burning as lasting across winter. Rewrite as "Why do the Northcove lanterns burn throughout the winter?": our translator has a proper whole-extent relation for "throughout" (and "during"/"while") but none for "through", so that one word swap keeps the season-long force without changing what you are asking.
Why did eleven lanterns on the Middle Row go out before dawn on day 16 of Year 1?

good. the count of eleven, the Middle Row restriction, the phrasal "go out" kept whole, the before-dawn bound and the day 16 / Year 1 date are all carried, and the line asks only for the reason the lanterns went out.
Why does the Council redistribute mire-essence reserves?
good. the query asks why the redistributing happens, with the Council as the doer and the mire-essence reserves as what is moved, and it adds nothing the question did not ask.
Why did the Council discuss burning wintergloss at the Stilllight Lantern in Year 1?

mixed: the query asks the right thing — the reason for the Council's discussing, with the lantern as place, Year 1 and the past tense all bound — but "discuss burning wintergloss" puts a gerund clause in the direct-object slot, which the translator has no rule for: here the burning is spelled out as an event in its own right, while a statement of the same fact may instead tuck it inside the discussing, and then the question matches nothing. Rewrite as "Why did the Council discuss the burning of wintergloss at the Stilllight Lantern in Year 1?" — an "of"-phrase after the noun is the shape the translator handles, so the question and the stored fact come out the same way.
Why does a Keeper harvest salt-bloom at the new moon?
(: $prf (And (Member $e harvest) (Agent $e $k) (Member $k keeper) (Theme $e salt_bloom) (Inheritance salt_bloom bloom) (Time $e new_moon) (ReasonFor $r $e)) $tv)

good. the query asks for the reason behind the harvesting itself, with the keeper bound as the agent, salt-bloom as what is harvested, and no tense marking on the habitual present; "at the new moon" rides the time slot as a plain recurring-occasion symbol, the same way a habitual's slot is normally recorded.
Why does the harvest party harvest salt-bloom at the new-moon spring tide?

good. the question is asked as the harvesting event plus a single "what was the reason" slot, with the harvest party bound by its kind and nothing asserted; the adjudicator reviewed the plain "new-moon spring tide" time symbol and ruled it acceptable — it fills the right slot and claims nothing extra.
Why does the village cremate the dead?

good. the query asks for the reason the village cremates, with the village bound by its kind as the one doing it and "the dead" as the non-specific thing cremated, no tense on the habitual present, and the reason left as the only open slot.
Why did a wraith emerge from the water of the Sunken Cove on day 120 of Year 1?

bad: "the water of the Sunken Cove" is asked for as water *contained in* the cove, but an "of"-phrase like this is stored as a part-of/belongs-to link instead, so the question looks for a connection no statement of that same phrase would have recorded and can come back empty even when the fact is in the knowledge base. Rewrite as "Why did a wraith emerge from the water in the Sunken Cove on day 120 of Year 1?" — the explicit "in" states the containment the question is already asking about, so statement and question agree. One residual caveat, harmless here: "day 120 of Year 1" names no month, so the day number is filed in the ordinary calendar-day slot — the same on both sides, so it still matches.
Why did the wraith turn away from the Stilllight Lantern on day 120 of Year 1?

good. the query rebuilds the turn-away event exactly as the question states it — the wraith as the one turning, the named Stilllight Lantern as what it turned away from, and day 120 of Year 1 as the time — and asks only for the reason, asserting nothing.
Why did the thread harvest at the West Row fall in Year 1?

mixed: nothing is lost and the query does ask for the reason of the fall, but the wording leaves two things to chance — "fall" reads either as a drop in yield or as "took place in Year 1", and a place phrase hung on the harvest noun ("the thread harvest at the West Row") has no settled encoding, so the row link is recorded here in a different shape from your parallel Middle Row question and the two will not match each other. If you mean the yield dropped, write "Why did the West Row thread harvest decline in Year 1?"; if you mean the harvest was held then, write "Why did the West Row thread harvest take place in Year 1?" — the named premodifier gives the row one fixed encoding either way.
Why did the thread harvest at the Middle Row fall on day 17 of Year 1?

bad: "fall on day 17 of Year 1" was taken literally — the query invents a separate falling event with the harvest as its object and puts the date on that falling, so it asks the reason for a fall rather than the reason the harvest was on day 17. Date the harvest with a plain light verb instead: "Why did the thread harvest at the Middle Row take place on day 17 of Year 1?" If you actually meant the yield dropped that day, say so with an unambiguous verb: "Why did the thread harvest at the Middle Row decline on day 17 of Year 1?"
Why does a surviving nightmoth flee to a dim lantern in the Hollows?

good. the query asks for the reason of the fleeing itself, keeps "surviving" and "dim" as plain descriptions of the moth and the lantern, uses the goal sense of "to" for a lantern it flees toward, and binds "Hollows" by its name alone. The reviewer's worry that "in the Hollows" might belong to the lantern rather than to the fleeing was judged not a defect — both attachments are licensed and the question is asked faithfully either way — so no rewrite is needed.
Why did the wraith response use half of the autumn feather store in Year 1?

good. the query builds the using event with the wraith response as the user and a half-portion of the autumn feather store as what was used, keeps Year 1 and the past tense, and asks only for the reason.
Why do the villagers consider the Cove Stair unlucky?

good. the query asks for the reason of the villagers' considering event, binding the villagers as a group of villagers and the Cove Stair by its name, and it keeps the "unlucky" verdict sealed inside the attitude, so the question asks what the villagers hold without asserting that the stair is unlucky.
Why does the village need sky-cats?

good. the needing is asked as an event with the village as the one who needs and sky-cats as what is needed, the habitual present adds no tense constraint that a stored fact would have to match, and the reason is the only open slot.
Why did the Council discuss the sky-cat drought in Year 1?

good. the query asks for the reason of the Council's discussing, keeps the sky-cat drought as the thing discussed (unchanged by being discussed), and pins the discussion to Year 1 in the past, so every part of the question is carried.
Why did Coraline Ash write in her log that a crowd of nightmoths brings sky-cats down from the cliff-spires?

(: $prf (And (Member $w write) (Experiencer $w $c) (Name $c "Coraline Ash") (Member $lg log) (Possession $lg $c) (Location $w $lg) (Past $w) (Theme $w (And (Member $cr crowd) (GroupOf $cr night_moth) (Member $bd bring_down) (Agent $bd $cr) (Theme $bd sky_cat) (Source $bd $sp))) (Inheritance night_moth moth) (GroupOf $sp cliff_spire) (Inheritance cliff_spire spire) (Inheritance sky_cat cat) (ReasonFor $r $w)) $tv)

good. the reason is asked of Coraline Ash's writing, not of the moths' behaviour, which is what the question means, and the claim she wrote stays sealed under the writing event so the query never asserts it; the log, the moths and the cliff-spires are all bound as the question names them.
Why does an apprentice's solo count reset when the apprentice's lantern dims?

mixed: the pieces are right (the reset and the dimming are both named, one apprentice is shared by "an apprentice" and "the apprentice", and the dimming is tied to the reset as the occasion), but the present-tense generic wording — "an apprentice's ... when ... dims" — makes the question ask why a standing REGULARITY holds, and a regularity is stored as a rule with no occurrence for the reason to hang on, so the query can only answer if some particular reset happens to be on file with a stated reason. Ask about a particular occasion instead, one finite clause per event: "Why did the apprentice's solo count reset when the apprentice's lantern dimmed?"
Why did the Council build the Stilllight Lantern sixty-three years ago?
(: $prf (And (Member $e build) (Agent $e $c) (Member $c council) (Patient $e $l) (Name $l "Stilllight Lantern") (Member $l lantern) (Past $e) (BeforeBy $e now 63 year) (ReasonFor $r $e)) $tv)

good. the query names the building event plainly, binds the Council by kind and the Stilllight Lantern by its name, keeps "sixty-three years ago" as a measured gap back from now, and leaves the reason as the one thing asked for.
Why does the sea-water store draw from the deep ebb?

good. the drawing is named as the focus event with the sea-water store as the one doing it and the deep ebb in the "from" slot, and the reason is the only unknown; the definite singular subject keeps this a plain standing fact rather than a rule, so a stated reason can actually attach to it.
Why does the Stilllight Keeper check the flame at midnight?
good. the query binds the Stilllight Keeper by name, puts the flame in the checked slot, keeps "at midnight" as a named time point the way dawn or noon would be stored, and asks only for the reason.
Why did the Stilllight Lantern burn dim on the night of day 111 of Year 1?

good. the burning is named as the focus event with the Stilllight Lantern bound by name, the whole "night of day 111 of Year 1" stack kept as separate time atoms, and "dim" kept as a state the lantern was in rather than a manner adverb; the reason is the only thing asked for.
Why does the Council meet at the Watch?

good. the query asks for the reason of the Council's meeting, treats the Council as one body doing the meeting rather than as separate members, and puts "at the Watch" on the meeting itself; the unmarked present is read as a standing practice, which is what the question intends.
Why does the harvest party need a spring tide?

good. the query builds the needing state with the harvest party as its experiencer and a spring tide as what is needed, binds both by kind, and hangs the asked-for reason on that event -- nothing of the question is lost or added.
Why does Old Vesh remember two bad winters?

good. Old Vesh is found by name, remembering is treated as a state he is in with the winters as what he remembers, and "two bad winters" keeps the count of two on the pair while "bad" is said of each winter separately — the same shape a statement of the same content would take.
Why did Brindle Coombe say at the Council that a hard winter would force the village to dim some lanterns?

(: $prf (And (Member $e say) (Experiencer $e $b) (Name $b "Brindle Coombe") (Location $e $c) (Member $c council) (Theme $e (And (Member $w winter) (Member $w hard) (Member $f force) (Agent $f $w) (Theme $f $d) (Future $f) (Member $d dim) (Agent $d $v) (Theme $d $l) (GroupOf $l lantern))) (Member $v village) (Past $e) (ReasonFor $r $e)) $tv)

bad: the query rebuilds the whole reported claim as one sealed block and puts the lanterns in the dimming's 'moved, unchanged' slot, but dimming changes the lanterns, so a faithfully parsed statement files them in the change-of-state slot instead and this question binds nothing. On top of that, a sealed two-event complement (a hard winter forcing, the village dimming) is matched as a single structural term whose conjunct order nothing fixes, so even a slot-correct version of this question can fail to line up with the statement. Keep the reported claim to one finite clause so the sealed content is small and stable: "Why did Brindle Coombe say at the Council that the village would have to dim some lanterns in a hard winter?"
Why does Hesper boil silken threads in sea-water?
good. the query names its focus event plainly -- Hesper as the boiler, the silken threads as what is boiled, sea-water as where -- and asks only for that event's reason, adding nothing.
A sky-cat hunts nightmoths at a lantern-row on the Cliff Path.
What happens to the nightmoth crowd at that lantern-row?
good. the hunting, its sky-cat hunter and nightmoth prey, the lantern-row as where it happens, and Cliff Path as a name with its own kind fact all land where they should.

bad: two things block it. "What happens to" never names the verb, so the translator cannot tell which slot the moths belong in and falls back on guessing two of them, and "the nightmoth crowd" has nothing to attach to, because the first sentence records the moths as a kind rather than as a particular set; the lantern-row also ends up recorded as where the crowd sits instead of where the happening is. Ask it from the actor's side, which does parse: "What does the sky-cat do at that lantern-row?" — that reaches the hunting at that lantern-row, whose prey is the nightmoths. If you need the moths themselves referable later, introduce them as a set in the first sentence: "A sky-cat hunts a crowd of nightmoths at a lantern-row on the Cliff Path."
A lantern at the Sunken Cove dies before dawn.
What emerges from the water of the Sunken Cove?

good. the lantern, the Sunken Cove as a named place with its kind, the lantern's position there, the dying, and the "before dawn" deadline are all carried, and no tense is invented for the bare present.

good. it asks for whatever emerges, with the cove's water as what it emerges from, and it reuses the Sunken Cove from the previous sentence instead of re-identifying it. One caution rather than a rewrite: it looks for the emerging thing as the doer of the emergence, so an answering sentence that presents it as carried or pushed up rather than moving under its own power would file it in a different slot and the question would miss it.
A lantern burns wintergloss alongside mire-essence.

mixed: the lantern burning wintergloss is recorded correctly, but "alongside mire-essence" only lands as a loose "alongside" modifier on the burning, so nothing says the mire-essence is burned too and the second substance drops out of the fuel claim. Rewrite as "A lantern burns wintergloss and mire-essence." — coordinated objects each get their own burning, so both substances are recorded as burned.

good. it asks what wintergloss does, and it uses the wintergloss symbol from the previous sentence directly instead of re-identifying it. One caution rather than a rewrite: the question asks for wintergloss as the doer, while your own premise stores it only as the substance being burned, so nothing will answer unless the knowledge base elsewhere has wintergloss acting.
A Keeper grinds feathers and scatters the feathers around a lit lantern at the Sunken Cove.
A wraith emerges from the water of the Sunken Cove.

good. each clause gets its own event with the Keeper acting and one shared set of feathers, "lit" stays a property of the lantern, and the genuinely ambiguous "at the Sunken Cove" is recorded as two complete readings — the scattering there, or the lantern there — rather than guessed.
good. the wraith, the emerging, the water it comes out of and that water's link to the cove are all there, and the cove reuses the symbol the first sentence created.

bad: "happens to" is recorded as a directed-at preposition, which no statement about something befalling the lantern would ever produce, so the question matches nothing — and with the verb unnamed there is no other slot the translator could have used. Ask it from the actor's side: "What does the wraith do?" parses cleanly and returns the next event. If the lantern's fate is what you need, name the verb — "Does the wraith put out the lantern?" — because which slot the lantern takes depends on that verb.
An apprentice's lantern dims during the apprentice's solo nights.
What happens to the apprentice's solo count?

bad: "during the apprentice's solo nights" is not carried — it lands in a plain time slot that takes calendar terms, not a set of nights, and even the correct "during" record is only defined over one single happening, so the recurring frame the sentence states is lost. Rewrite it as one occurrence per night: "Whenever an apprentice works a solo night, that apprentice's lantern dims." — that gives a dimming for each solo night, tied to it. Separately, "solo" is being asserted as a property of the night, which it is not; "a night the apprentice works alone" avoids that if you want to keep the wording literal.

bad: "happens to" again lands as a directed-at preposition rather than in a slot for the thing something befalls, so it matches nothing, and "the apprentice's solo count" has nothing to bind to either — a count is held as the size of a set of things, never as a thing of its own. Ask about the nights themselves: "How many solo nights has the apprentice had?" If you mean the count changing, name the change: "Does the apprentice's count of solo nights rise?"
A cold wind strikes the Cliff Path at night.
A lantern on the Cliff Path is unprepared.
What happens to the unprepared lantern?

good. the wind gets its own thing to hang facts on, the striking carries its doer, the path it strikes and the night it happens at, and the named Cliff Path is kept as one name with "path" stated as its kind.

good. the lantern is a fresh thing rather than anything carried over from the first sentence, "on the Cliff Path" keeps the surface "on" instead of claiming the lantern sits inside the path, and "unprepared" is recorded as a plain property of it.

bad: the query hangs the lantern off a "to" oblique — the slot for what an action is aimed at — so it never asks what befalls the lantern and can match nothing in the knowledge base; an open "what happens to X?" has no supported form at all, because the slot an answer would file X in depends on the verb the question leaves unnamed. Name the event you are asking about and give the lantern its plain object position, with no "to"-phrase: "Does the cold wind damage the unprepared lantern at night?" If you would rather keep the question open, ask it from the acting side, which is supported: "What does the cold wind do at night?"
A cold wind strikes the Cliff Path at night.
A lantern on the Cliff Path is salt-bloomed.
What happens to the salt-bloomed lantern?
good. the cold wind, the striking, the struck Cliff Path and the night it happens at are all carried, and the multi-word name stays one symbol with "path" stated separately as its kind.

good. the Cliff Path is reused from the first sentence rather than introduced a second time, "on" is kept as the surface position rather than read as containment, and "salt-bloomed" is carried as one plain property of the lantern.
